title: WebSeer: Training Deeper Search Agents through Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection
one_liner: Train a search agent to stop, inspect its last move, and correct itself before the next search step so longer search chains stay useful.
lead: A search agent answers a hard question by issuing searches, opening pages, reading results, and deciding what to do next. The hard part is not the first step. The hard part is keeping many steps aligned with the question. WebSeer adds a structured self-check during training so the agent learns when a step failed, why it failed, and what the next step should change.

problem.h2: Why long search chains fall apart
paras: A web search agent usually works in rounds. It reads the question, sends a search, opens a result, extracts facts, and decides the next move. Early moves can look fine even when they quietly push the agent off track. After several rounds, the small mistakes pile up, and the final answer is wrong because the agent spent its budget on the wrong pages.

A plain reinforcement learning setup tells the agent whether the final answer was right, but that signal arrives too late. The agent does not get much help on the middle steps where the real damage happens. So it learns shallow behavior: a few safe search moves, then a guess.

callout.html: WebSeer teaches the agent to review each search step during training so the next step is adjusted before errors spread through the whole search chain.

paras: The paper changes the training signal for a search agent. Instead of rewarding only the final answer, it inserts reflection traces that explain what went wrong in the current step and what should change next.
object.object: the training trace for each search round

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: step quality over time
hidden.name: how much each new step still helps the answer
paras: The paper is really measuring whether later search steps still add useful evidence. A long chain is only valuable when each extra move raises the chance of finding the right facts. If later steps mostly repeat weak searches or chase side topics, the chain is deep in length but shallow in value.

WebSeer raises this hidden quantity by making the agent state what the last step achieved, what evidence is still missing, and how the next move should target that gap. That training pattern matters because it turns each extra round into a chance to repair the chain instead of just extending it.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark places where reflection can change the next move enough to keep later rounds useful.

reads.html: The method wants each added search round to still move the agent closer to the answer.
The system trains on reflection-annotated trajectories so the policy can detect step-level errors and revise later tool choices.

paras: The core problem is delayed credit. When the agent gets only a final reward, it cannot easily tell which search move helped and which one hurt. Reflection inserts an explicit description of the current gap. That helps because the next decision is conditioned on a summary of the mistake, not only on raw search history.

The two-stage training setup matters for the same reason. The cold-start phase shows the model examples of useful reflective behavior, so early training does not wander randomly. The reinforcement learning phase then keeps the good reflection pattern and strengthens the parts that raise answer accuracy. Together they push the agent toward longer chains that remain coherent because each new move is informed by a concrete diagnosis of the last one.

stages.s: write a reflection on missing or wrong evidence
choose the next action using that reflection
longer search chain with fewer wasted rounds

math.h2: A compact way to score deeper search
math.words: total training value = answer reward plus a weighted bonus for useful reflections across all search rounds
symbols: reward for producing the correct final answer
how strongly reflection quality affects training
how much the reflection at round t improves the later search path

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the agent answers correctly, so answer reward is 1.0.
There are three reflective rounds with gains 0.2, 0.1, and 0.3 because each one redirects the next search step toward better evidence.
Set lambda to 0.5. Then total value is 1.0 + 0.5 x (0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3) = 1.3.
A chain with the same final answer but empty or useless reflections would receive a lower value, so training prefers the chain that stays informative over more rounds.

math.note: The exact form in the paper may differ, but this captures the idea that answer quality and reflection quality are trained together.

bars.h2: What better search depth should look like

charts.title: Without reflection training
charts.note: Late search steps often repeat earlier mistakes because the agent has no structured way to review them.

charts.title: With reflection training
charts.note: Useful reflection lowers repetition because the agent names the missing evidence before the next search move.

items.b: Reflection text can become empty ritual.
items.html: If the review step says generic things such as "search more" without naming the missing fact, it does not help the next action because the diagnosis is too vague.

items.b: Bad search results can still trap the agent.
items.html: When the web result set is poor, the agent may reflect correctly yet still have no good page to open. Reflection improves choice among visible options because it can redirect the next action toward the best available lead, but it cannot create evidence that the search engine did not surface.

items.b: Long chains can drift into self-confirmation.
items.html: If the reflection step only repeats the current belief, later searches may keep supporting the same wrong idea. The review must mention missing evidence or conflicts so the next step can challenge the current path.
Reflection helps when it points to a specific evidence gap, because that gives the next search move a concrete target such as a missing date, source, or entity.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small search environment around a multi-hop question set. Let one agent search and answer directly. Let a second agent insert one review step after each search result: what was learned, what is missing, and what the next search should target. Keep the same model size and search budget for both systems.
Log the full search chain for each question. Count how many later rounds introduce new evidence, how often a round merely repeats an earlier search, and whether the final answer is correct.
demo.metric_eq: useful_late_round_rate = later rounds that add new evidence / all later rounds
demo.closing: The demo should show that reflection raises answer quality because it turns the next search step toward an explicit missing fact, so later rounds add evidence instead of repeating the same search.
